lens: Arabic linguistics & classical balaghah — voice (active/passive), form classification, lexical precision, hapax legomena, verb-choice across retellings; grammar-claim vs literary-claim kept marked

proposals.title: You Shove the Orphan Away. The Same Verb Shoves You Into the Fire.
proposals.thesis: The rough physical verb 'to shove' (root د-ع-ع) is used as a verb only twice in the whole Quran. In Surah al-Ma'un it is active — the person who 'shoves the orphan away.' In Surah at-Tur it turns passive — the same people 'are shoved toward the Fire with a shove.' The grammar itself delivers the sentence: the hand that pushes becomes the body that is pushed, one verb doing both.

personas.note: The payoff lands with zero Arabic prerequisite — 'same verb, active then passive' is a sentence any parent can say to a teenager. Sara can WhatsApp it verbatim; Khalil gets a clean, verifiable root census (2 verb tokens, 1 other non-verb token).

proposals.risks: Scope must be stated exactly: 2 verb tokens across 2 verses; the root has 1 further non-verb token, so 'used only twice' must specify 'as a verb.' Do not call the sound of the doubled 'ayn violent — that is folk-phonetics; the point is morphological (active vs passive of one lemma), not acoustic.
proposals.why_now: A voice-flip article already performs on the site (the funeral-verb piece). This is the strongest untouched case: it carries a moral edge (orphan care) that reads as measure-for-measure justice built into the grammar, exactly the contested-adjacent, shareable register the audience arrives on.

proposals.title: Two Places the Quran Drops the Doer: Paradise, and the Forbidden Meat
proposals.thesis: The passive voice hides who acts, and the Quran uses it deliberately in two opposite directions. Every time it describes the saved being adorned with jewelry (root ح-ل-ي, four verb tokens, all passive) the people never dress themselves — they 'are adorned.' Every time it forbids meat 'dedicated to other than God' (root ه-ل-ل as a verb, four tokens, all passive) it never names who did the dedicating. One passive lifts a reward you did not hand yourself; the other buries the false invoker so his name is never spoken.

personas.note: This is a genuine balaghah teaching — the passive as agent-suppression doing two jobs. Khalil and Yusuf get a citable 4-of-4 / 4-of-4 census and a classical category (hadhf al-fa'il). Lower for Sara/Amina because the reward is conceptual, not narrative.

proposals.risks: Must scope 'verb tokens only' for both roots — ح-ل-ي and ه-ل-ل each have non-verbal tokens (ornaments; the crescent/hilal sense). Keep the claim at the level of grammar (agent deletion), and mark plainly that the theological reading is an extension of the classical observation, not identical to it.
proposals.why_now: The site's own advisor note asks for a 'linguistic honesty' habit — grammar-claim marked apart from literary reading. This article is that habit made into content: one clean grammatical device (the passive), two verified data sets, and a payoff a reader can check against the corpus.

proposals.title: You Can't Line Yourself Up: The Army Verb That Becomes a Prayer for Gratitude
proposals.thesis: The verb 'to hold in ordered ranks' (root و-ز-ع) appears as a verb five times. In its passive it means being marshaled by a force outside you — Sulayman's hosts drawn up in ranks, and deniers herded toward the Fire. Its only two active uses are the identical prayer: 'My Lord, marshal me to be grateful for Your favor.' You cannot rank yourself into gratitude; you ask God to order your heart the way He orders armies. And that exact prayer is spoken by only two people in the Quran — Sulayman at the height of his kingdom, and an ordinary person reaching forty.

personas.note: The prayer is short, memorizable, and immediately usable — Sara and Amina can take it away as their own du'a. Khalil/Yusuf get the double reveal: the voice split (3 passive / 2 active) AND the word-for-word phrase twin across 27:19 and 46:15.

proposals.risks: Two insights share the same verses, so the article must not double-count them as separate proofs — it is one phenomenon (the active tokens ARE the prayer). State form-IV for the active tokens and scope the phrase claim to the exact contiguous string. No superlative on 'mightiest king'; say 'a king at the height of his power.'
proposals.why_now: It converts a grammar observation into a devotional takeaway without overreaching — the reader leaves with a verified prayer and a reason it is phrased the way it is. That combination (rigor plus something to hold) is the site's sweet spot and is currently unbuilt for this root.

proposals.title: 'Strike With Your Staff' Is Said Three Times — and the Water Word Is One the Quran Uses Nowhere Else
proposals.thesis: The command 'strike with your staff' appears in exactly three verses. Twice the target is a rock and the result is water; once the target is the sea and the result is dry land. Even the rock-tellings do not agree on the verb: al-Baqarah says the water 'burst out' (fanfajarat), while al-A'raf swaps in 'fanbajasat' — a trickle-word that appears in exactly one verse in the entire Quran. Same staff, same twelve springs; the Quran reaches for a word it never reuses to color one telling differently.

personas.note: The hapax (a word used exactly once) is catnip for Khalil and Yusuf and is fully verifiable. The mirror-miracle framing — strike stone, get water; strike water, get stone-hard ground — gives Sara and Amina a vivid line to carry.

proposals.risks: Overlap watch: two published pieces touch Musa's staff/sea thematically. This proposal's reveal is strictly lexical — the shared imperative appearing exactly 3 times and the forked result-verbs including the whole-Quran hapax inbajasa (7:160). Keep it on morphology/lexicon, not on retelling the narrative, to stay clear of the existing articles.
proposals.why_now: It is the cleanest hapax case in the pool, and hapax legomena are a documented content vein the site wants to mine in the AI era. Corpus tools now let a reader confirm 'one verse, one time' in seconds — the article's whole claim is independently checkable.

proposals.title: Ibrahim's Wife Laughed in One Surah. In Another, She Slapped Her Own Face.
proposals.thesis: When the angels tell Ibrahim's wife she will have a son, the Quran gives her two different reactions in two tellings. In Surah Hud she 'laughed'; in adh-Dhariyat she 'came forward in a clamor and struck her own face,' calling herself a barren old woman. The verb for that slap (root ص-ك-ك) is used exactly once in the whole Quran — the Quran keeps a word in reserve for the one gesture no other moment needed.

personas.note: A woman's startled, human reaction to impossible news — highly relatable and shareable for Amina and Sara. Khalil gets a second hapax to verify. Slightly lower for Yusuf since the payoff is narrative-emotional more than argumentative.

proposals.risks: Do not harmonize the two reactions into a single event or claim contradiction — the honest frame is 'two tellings, two facets of one moment.' Scope the hapax as 'root ص-ك-ك, exactly one verse (51:29).' Avoid reading tone into the laugh beyond what the text supports.
proposals.why_now: No published article covers this annunciation reaction, and it opens the underused territory of women's voices in the narrative with a verifiable linguistic anchor rather than sentiment. It is teen-readable and travels well on messaging apps.

proposals.title: Watch the Verb Flip: When a Human Wins, the Grammar Hands the Win to God
proposals.thesis: Several verbs in the Quran appear only a handful of times, and their voice flips in a consistent direction. When believers rout an army, the verb stays active but is chained to 'by God's leave'; elsewhere the same verb goes fully passive and the human victor disappears. A denier is 'struck dumb' (passive); the hypocrites 'are plunged back' into the trap while God 'reverts them' (active); people 'are turned upside down' while God 'sets back in creation' whomever He gives long life. Read together, the grammar keeps handing the agency to God — every time a human could take the credit, the voice removes it.

personas.note: A corpus-survey piece for the rigor readers — each root is a verified 2-token census and the pattern is checkable end to end. Lower for Sara/Amina because it is a pattern-across-verses argument, not a single scene.

proposals.risks: This must NOT become a phonetic-symbolism piece — rakasa and nakasa sound alike but that is not the claim; the claim is voice + shared meaning of reversal, and I would state explicitly that the resemblance is not being read as sound-symbolism. Scope each root as 'verb tokens' (several have separate noun tokens: buhtan, sa'iqa). Present each case, then the pattern; do not overstate it as a universal rule of Quranic grammar.
proposals.why_now: The voice-flip genre already works on the site, but only as one-verse pieces; no article has surveyed the pattern itself. AI-era corpus access is exactly what makes a multi-root survey verifiable and citable — the piece models the site's methodology-transparency goal while giving MSA and student readers something to cite.
